confidence_why: Shiraishi's 2006 first-hand phonology of West-Sakhalin Nivkh (Amur dialect group) fixes stress on the first syllable of the stem, and the only dissent is Panfilov's 1962 report of a few Amur words with non-initial stress (umˈgu 'woman', utˈku 'man'), which Shiraishi's own speakers stress initially, while Kreinovich's 1979 final-constituent stress concerns Sakhalin-dialect compounds and phrases, not words.
catalog_quote: In WSN, stress is fixed on the first syllable in a polysyllabic stem. Phonetic correlates of stress are the assignment of high pitch in the citation form and for some speakers palatalization of the consonant before front vowels /i, e/

new_statements.quote: In WSN, stress is fixed on the first syllable in a polysyllabic stem.10 Phonetic correlates of stress are the assignment of high pitch in the citation form and for some speakers palatalization of the consonant before front vowels /i, e/ (see section 2.1.4). [...] There are no special stress patterns which distinguish compounds (25a) from phrases (25b-e). In both structures it is the first constituent which receives primary stress in WSN.11 [fn. 10:] Panfilov states that in the Amur dialect stress may fall on a non-initial syllable in some words and cite examples as [umˈgu] 'woman' and [utˈku] 'man' (Panfilov 1962: 22). In the speech of my informants, these forms are always initially stressed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the first syllable of a polysyllabic stem (examples ˈmorqa- 'to live', ˈcaqo 'knife', ˈoɬa 'child', ˈoɬa-gu 'children'); its phonetic correlates are high pitch on the citation form and, for some speakers, palatalization of a consonant before a stressed /i, e/. In compounds and in phrases alike the first constituent carries the primary stress (ˈɲaɲ ajs 'glasses', ˈpilkar ŋɨɲk 'a big face'). Vowel length is not contrastive and lengthening is independent of stress (p. 21); epenthetic vowels in Russian loanwords bear stress, but epenthetic vowels in clitics never do (p. 30, section 2.6). Note: the extracted text dump renders the stress mark and some IPA symbols from the phonetic font as ¥, ¢, Õ etc; the prose quoted is verbatim, the example transcriptions above are my rendering.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated as such; the text speaks only of 'primary stress' on the first constituent of compounds and phrases, which implies weaker stress on later constituents, but no secondary-stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the West-Sakhalin dialect itself: 'stress is fixed'. Cross-dialect reports in the footnotes: fn. 10, Panfilov (1962: 22) gives some non-initially stressed words in the Amur dialect ([umˈgu] 'woman', [utˈku] 'man'), which Shiraishi's WSN informants stress initially; fn. 11, 'Kreinovich reports that in the Sakhalin dialect the last constituent receives stress in compounds and noun phrases: [cʰo ˈzoŋqr] "head of fish" (Kreinovich 1979: 298)', i.e. the opposite constituent from WSN at phrase level.
new_statements.identity_note: Shiraishi 2006 describes the West-Sakhalin dialect of Nivkh (WSN; his own fieldwork data), not Gilyak/Nivkh as a whole; its footnotes summarise other dialects second-hand (Amur per Panfilov 1962; Sakhalin per Kreinovich 1979). The catalog's Gordon record gives no dialect.

new_statements.quote: [p. 263] Stress is not phonemic. It tends to fall on the first vowel of a word but it is bound to the morphemes of the imperative and vocative (ylyj, yta 'father!'; pfyja 'come!') and is very frequently associated with certain emphatic verbal mor-phemes (pfy=nd=ra 'he came, indeed'). [p. 277] Stress falls, as it does in standard words, on the first vowel; certain redu-plicated forms may carry it on the second vowel ( 40, 46, 51, 53, 54).

Adds (i) explicit non-contrastiveness, (ii) morphological exceptions not on record (imperative/vocative suffixes stressed, emphatic morphemes attract stress, second-vowel stress in some reduplicated nursery forms), (iii) a different variety: southeastern (East) Sakhalin dialect, 1950s, one speaker, versus Shiraishi's West-Sakhalin. new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and as a rule falls on the first vowel (first syllable) of the word; it is however tied to the imperative and vocative morphemes (which carry it, e.g. yta 'father!', pfyja 'come!') and is often attracted to emphatic verbal morphemes; nursery words follow the same initial-stress rule, except that some reduplicated nursery forms have stress on the second vowel. Variety: southeastern Sakhalin dialect, idiolect of one informant (Mrs. Tiyoko Nakamura, b. 1906 near Siska), recorded in Abashiri, Japan.
new_statements.exceptions: imperative and vocative morphemes bear the stress (ylyj/yta 'father!', pfyja 'come!'); emphatic verbal morphemes frequently attract it (pfy=nd=ra 'he came, indeed'); certain reduplicated nursery forms (items 40, 46, 51, 53, 54) carry stress on the second vowel; vowel quantity only in numerals and a few morphemes
new_statements.identity_note: Austerlitz 1956 treats Gilyak (Nivkh) nursery vocabulary, reportedly from Sakhalin speakers he worked with in Japan; the catalog statement held by the project (Shiraishi 2006) describes the West-Sakhalin dialect. Variety of the p. 263 remark could not be checked.

tone_statements.quote: Ударение разноместное и подвижное. Может выполнять смыслоразличительную функцию: [...] ‘называет/называл’ — [...] ‘сушит/сушил’. Некоторые морфемы, при помощи которых образуются формы слов, всегда являются ударными. Это, например, показатели императива у глагола: [...] ‘иди’, [...] ‘идите’, и суффикс звательной формы у имени существительного: [...] ‘мать’ (обращение). В одних и тех же словах в различных диалектах ударение иногда не совпадает: [...] (амур.) — [...] (вост.-сахал.) ‘ходит/ходил пешком’. Высказывается гипотеза о существовании в Н.я. тоновых противопоставлений.
tone_statements.translation: Stress is free (not bound to a fixed position) and mobile. It can distinguish meaning: [...] 'names/named' vs [...] 'dries/dried'. Some morphemes used to build word forms are always stressed, e.g. the imperative markers of the verb ([...] 'go!', [...] 'go! (pl.)') and the vocative suffix of the noun ([...] 'mother!' (address)). In the same words the stress sometimes does not coincide across dialects: [...] (Amur) vs [...] (East Sakhalin) 'walks/walked'. A hypothesis has been advanced that tonal oppositions exist in Nivkh.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between the sources opened and the catalog: Shiraishi 2006 (West-Sakhalin Nivkh) states fixed initial stress on the polysyllabic stem, which matches Gordon's fixed: initial syllable record. Within Shiraishi's footnotes there is reported dialect variation, not a conflict of the catalog reading: Panfilov (1962: 22) lists a few Amur-dialect words with non-initial stress ([umˈgu], [utˈku]) that Shiraishi's own informants stress initially, and Kreinovich (1979: 298) reports final-constituent stress in Sakhalin compounds and noun phrases where WSN has first-constituent stress; the latter is a phrase-level, not word-level, difference. Austerlitz 1956 could not be opened, so its p. 263 stress remark remains unverified.

sources.note: Reconstructs the Proto-Nivkh accent system and vocalism by loanword analysis and internal reconstruction; argues that the place of the Proto-Nivkh accent depended on vowel height and syllable structure and that unstressed-vowel loss (which reshaped phonotactics, consonantism and morphophonology) postdates the break-up of the modern varieties. The abstract frames accent as stress placement and does not mention tone; whether the body addresses the older hypothesis of tonal oppositions (Kreinovich/Panfilov era, reported by Gruzdeva 1997: 141) is not established.
